procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 5, 1967, of the Madras High Court in Criminal Appeal Nos. 34 to 38 of 1965, which acquitted the accused.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The convicted accused appealed to the Madras High Court. The Public Prosecutor filed a petition for enhancement of sentence in the High Court. The High Court acquitted the accused and dismissed the petition for enhancement of sentence. The Public Prosecutor applied to the High Court under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution for a certificate of fitness to appeal to the Supreme Court, but this application was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Deputy Chief Controller of Imports & Exports, the original complainant, secured special leave to appeal from the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution against the High Court's order of acquittal. The respondents (originally the accused) raised a preliminary objection to the competency of the appeal, arguing that the Deputy Chief Controller lacked locus standi because the Public Prosecutor had applied to the High Court for the necessary certificate. The Supreme Court had to decide whether special leave to appeal could be granted to the appellant when he did not move the High Court and whether the respondents were guilty of the offenses charged.

issue.issue_text: Whether special leave to appeal could be granted to the appellant when he did not move the High Court.

facts: The appellant, the Deputy Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, was the original complainant in the case.
After the High Court acquitted the accused, the Public Prosecutor applied to the High Court for a certificate for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court, but this application was dismissed.
The appellant himself did not apply to the High Court, but instead directly sought and obtained special leave to appeal from the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The respondents raised a preliminary objection, arguing that the appellant had no right (locus standi) to apply for special leave because he had not first moved the High Court for a certificate.
law: There is no provision of law that disentitles an original, lawfully authorized complainant from applying for special leave to the Supreme Court.
Article 136 of the Constitution and the Supreme Court Rules are wide enough to empower the Supreme Court to grant special leave in such cases.
application: The Court noted that the appellant was the duly authorized complainant who initiated the case.

The Court reasoned that the fact that the Public Prosecutor had filed a separate application in the High Court did not in any way prevent the appellant from seeking special leave from the Supreme Court.

The Court affirmed that its broad powers under Article 136 allowed it to grant special leave to the appellant in this situation, regardless of the Public Prosecutor's separate actions in the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondents' objection and held that special leave to appeal could be granted. The Court found no legal rule preventing the appellant, as the original complainant, from applying for special leave, and concluded that Article 136 provided ample authority for the Court to grant it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondents were guilty of the offences charged.

facts: The respondents were accused of violating the conditions of an import licence.

The appellant (Deputy Chief Controller of Imports and Exports) filed a complaint against the respondents (a company and several individuals) for offences under the Indian Penal Code and the Imports and Exports Control Act.
The trial court convicted most of the accused, but the High Court acquitted all of them on appeal.

The Supreme Court found that the respondents' own application for the import license demonstrated that the object and purpose of importing the item (a press) was for its resale, which was a breach of the license.
The Court determined that this breach was fully intended, designed, and deliberate.
law: The respondents were charged under s. 120-B of the Indian Penal Code (criminal conspiracy) and s. 5 of the Imports & Exports Act, 1947, read with cl. 5 of the Import Control Order, 1955.
The Court cited the authority of 'State of West Bengal v. Motilal Kanoria' to hold that individual accused persons can be held liable along with the company that holds the license.
application: The Court rejected the High Court's decision to acquit, stating that the High Court's view was not sustainable based on the statutory language and the Import Control Policy.

The Court found that the respondents were fully aware of the policy and that their own application was "proof positive" of their awareness and their deliberate intent to breach the license conditions.
The Court dismissed the argument that only the company, as the license holder, could be held liable. It affirmed that on the facts, both the company and the individual accused were guilty.
The Court emphasized the seriousness of the offense, noting that breaching import conditions prejudicially affects the country's national economy.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the respondents were guilty of the offences charged. It set aside the High Court's order of acquittal and convicted the accused individuals and the company, imposing fines on them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether special leave to appeal could be granted to the appellant when he did not move the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (Deputy Chief Controller of Imports and Exports) was the original complainant, duly authorized by statute to file the complaint.
The fact that the Public Prosecutor handled proceedings in the High Court does not disentitle the original complainant from applying for special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court.
There is no provision of law that deprives the lawfully authorized complainant of the right to seek special leave and prosecute the appeal.
Article 136 of the Constitution and the Supreme Court Rules are wide enough to empower the Court to grant special leave to the appellant in this case.
respondent_arguments: The special leave petition was filed by the Deputy Chief Controller of Imports & Exports, not by the State, which had conducted the prosecution.
The Public Prosecutor, not the Deputy Chief Controller, had applied to the High Court for the certificate to appeal.
Therefore, the Deputy Chief Controller has no locus standi (standing) to apply for special leave.
The special leave was granted on an incompetent petition and should be revoked.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondents were guilty of the offences charged.
appellant_arguments: The respondents violated clause (c) of their import licence by selling the printing press.
The respondents were guilty of offences under s. 120B I.P.C., s. 5 of the Imports and Exports Control Act, and cl. 5(iv) of the Imports Control Order, 1955.
respondent_arguments: Condition (c) of the licence related only to raw material or accessories.
The printing press that was sold was neither raw material nor an accessory.
Therefore, the sale of the printing press did not contravene the licence condition.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The meaning of words and phrases in a statute or legal instrument is not controlled by their dictionary definitions where the scheme of the instrument, considered as a whole, conveys a different meaning. The particular meaning of words should be gathered from the context, the nature of the subject matter, the purpose of the author, and the object to be achieved, rather than by dissecting the instrument and defining words in isolation.
obiter: Breach of conditions for import of goods is a serious matter because it prejudicially affects the country's national economy.

The Supreme Court has the power under Article 136 of the Constitution to convert an acquittal into a conviction, particularly when the High Court's view is not sustainable on the statutory language and policy.
When a company is the holder of a licence, individual persons involved can also be held liable for offences committed.
A duly authorized complainant under a statute, such as the Deputy Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, is entitled to apply for special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 136.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The respondents deliberately breached the conditions of their import license by reselling a printing press that they were permitted to import only for their own actual use. They secured the license by expressly representing that the press was for their newspaper's use, and their own application demonstrated full awareness of this condition. The High Court's view that the license condition was inapplicable was unsustainable, as the respondents' actions, including negotiating the sale before the press even arrived, showed a clear and deliberate intent to violate the terms of the license from the outset.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of Article 136 of the Constitution and the Supreme Court Rules to determine standing for a special leave petition, concluding they are 'wide enough' to empower the Court to grant leave to the original complainant even if the Public Prosecutor handled an earlier stage.

Interpretation of an import license's conditions in the context of the broader statutory framework, including the Imports and Exports Act, 1947, the Import Control Order, 1955, and the government's Import Control Policy.
The standard for converting an acquittal into a conviction under Article 136, which is permissible when the High Court's view is not sustainable on the statutory language and policy.
policy_considerations: Breach of conditions for import of goods is a serious matter because it prejudicially affects our country's national economy.
